newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish legislators near deal on new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Polish legislators near deal on new constitution.

text.p: After three years of hard debate, Poland's legislators on Wednesday neared a compromise deal on a new draft national constitution to replace the country's previous, discredited, communist-era document.

Members of the four largest parliamentary parties, in the legislature's constitutional committee, were thrashing out ways to skirt round differences so that the new constitution can stand a chance of passing before elections late this year.
The committee's chairman, Marek Mazurkiewicz of the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), said the committee might be able to submit an agreed draft this week.
The constitution must then pass through an assembly of both houses of parliament and be submitted to a national referendum.

"Within a month there could be a second reading, which would last some days. A third reading, under optimal conditions could be in March and then the possibility is open even for a referendum before the (summer) holidays," Mazurkiewicz told private Radio Zet on Wednesday morning.
If the constitution is not approved before general elections due in September or October, different parties might win the polls and work on the draft would begin afresh.
This would extend a process which has dragged on embarrassingly long after the 1989 fall of communism, leaving Poland's system based on a stopgap "small" constitution.
To avoid this, the main parliamentary opposition parties have been cooperating with the ruling coalition of ex-communists and Peasants to smoothe over differences.
On Wednesday, they got round a key dispute on whether the constitution should call for a new level of local government by avoiding the issue and asserting the goal of decentralisation.

But rightist, Catholic parties, which were so split that they failed to enter parliament in 1993 elections and therefore had little say on the draft, reject its secular tone and want the charter to be founded on religious ideas of "natural law".
These parties, notably a strong new alliance around the Solidarity trade union, plan to oppose the current draft during the referendum or maybe change it if they win the elections.

"I do not think this draft will...be acceptable to all," rightist deputy Jerzy Gwizdz told the radio, stressing that his camp, which opposed last year's law easing abortion, wanted protection of the unborn child to be in the constitution.
Solidarity submitted its own constitutional draft two years ago, and says it was signed by two million citizens.
Meanwhile, the two ruling parties, with the opposition centrist Union for Freedom and the leftist Labour Union, have compromised in the committee on various issues.

The Peasants and Labour Union won inclusion of guarantees of free basic health care for all, regardless of income, paid from public funds and free education, although the draft admits the possibility of some charges for higher state education.

Among other deals, the ex-communists agreed to slightly weaken the presidency, now held by their ally Aleksander Kwasniewski, by allowing his veto to be overruled by three fifths of lower house deputies rather than two-thirds.
